entities.name: The Grafts Brought to a Sleeping Island

value.title: The Grafts Brought to a Sleeping Island
value.summary: During the period of the Festival of Unfinished Journeys, Selucian boat crews and visiting growers recorded an agreement for a small orchard on an already familiar resting sea tortoise. Donated grafts commemorated journeys delayed or abandoned. The agreement limited loading and moorings; it did not claim ownership of the animal.

entities.name: The Jar Set Aside for Strangers

value.title: The Jar Set Aside for Strangers
value.summary: Carriers renewed a small daily reserve for travellers reaching the Rain Crown without adequate water. The decision followed a dispute over priority sales to a wealthy caravan. The reserve survives through contributions and public tallying, rather than a claim that the crown itself chooses worthy visitors.

value.title: The Crown Receives Woven Veils
value.summary: A long dry interval prompted cistern keepers to replace ineffective hanging cloth with woven copper-mesh mist catchers. Several fragments of the old tower were braced from the ground. The improvement made ordinary collection more dependable while leaving drought a real limit.

entities.name: Seven Languages at the Rain Crown

value.title: Seven Languages at the Rain Crown
value.summary: Travelling interpreters and water carriers recorded a shared allocation at the already ancient cistern beneath Orovant's hovering crown. The work reflected the same practical problems of translation then being debated in the Market of Borrowed Tongues. Its surviving tablets promise measured water when available, never command of the weather.

entities.name: The Keys Hung on the Skyharp

value.title: The Keys Hung on the Skyharp
value.summary: During the gradual departures remembered as the Winter of Returned Keys, some Hazelstairs families left labelled keys with the hoist keeper while travelling downhill. The keys were intended for neighbours needing shelter or tools. Later commemorative ribbons inherited their place on the surviving frame.

entities.name: The Hoist Below the Griffin Ledge

value.title: The Hoist Below the Griffin Ledge
value.summary: In the final years of the Juniper Gate griffin response, carriers reused an older stone lifting frame to move quarry supplies along a less disruptive slope. The surviving works ledger includes payments to egg-watchers and compensation for lost animals. It does not describe the frame as a bridge across the gorge.

entities.name: A Weather Voice for the Winter Rooms

value.title: A Weather Voice for the Winter Rooms
value.summary: Porters working during the Winter Latch improvements fitted resonators to the retired hoist cables. Their signals helped nearby keepers compare winds and organise guarded departures. The musical adaptation belonged to the lower shelter network; it never completed the giant stair's missing upper span.

value.title: The Gauge Beside the Wonder
value.summary: A public inspection reopened arguments about who actually received water from the Upward Fall. Workers installed an ordinary gauge beside the spectacular stream and posted the maintenance rota. The gauge, rather than the height of the spray, became the basis for the current distribution hearing.

value.title: The Fall Survives Its Aqueduct
value.summary: An aqueduct section failed after years of neglected repairs. Keepers shortened the receiving channel and stabilised one arch instead of rebuilding the larger scheme. The upward stream survived, but several farms lost their former connection and negotiated different water arrangements.

entities.name: A Small River Is Asked to Climb

value.title: A Small River Is Asked to Climb
value.summary: Amid the Open Sluices rebuilding debates, a group of millers funded a limited water-lifting experiment on a Vey side channel. Its receiving works were sized for irrigation and ordinary drainage. The agreement required the diversion to be closed during unsafe floods, preventing later claims that the new wonder could protect the entire basin.

value.title: The Lantern Concord Rose
value.summary: River thrones, port councils, judges, and record-keepers built a transcontinental order of roads, seals, shared measures, and enforceable obligations. It created real peace while teaching institutions to value what could be counted over what could not.

value.title: Caldris at the Threshold
value.summary: It is 643 AS, eighty-three years after the Three Banner War ended. Trade continues and harvests remain broadly adequate, although burdens and local shortages are uneven. Temporary tolls persist, counterfeit seven-sided seals support questionable claims, and physical dragon evidence is appearing in different regions for different reasons. The Lantern Sea Accord congress is due next year at Aster Quay, whose presiding chair is missing. Carrowmere shipwrights have justified concerns about the autumn grain fleet. Political households consider uncertain inheritances; village keepers consider roofs, fuel, and whether the next delivery will arrive before rain. Children still learn adapted versions of old tunes. Letters wait for carriers, gardens preserve fragile varieties, and repaired objects pass into new hands. At Bramblebridge, roads and households already have histories before any adventurer enters them.

entities.name: Two Funerals and Many New Claims

value.title: Two Funerals and Many New Claims
value.summary: Two unrelated royal heirs died within eighteen months of one another in separate accidents. The deaths altered calculations about marriages, succession, and lesser claims. Households far from either court encountered the consequences through postponed agreements, new envoys, and requests to locate old papers. Public grief and political opportunity occupied the same rooms. Some participants sincerely feared instability; others promoted claims that had attracted little attention when succession seemed settled. Rumour joined the deaths into a single pattern even where the available evidence did not. These events did not resolve Alderwick's concerns over its childless queen or the Veyr Marches' separate questions about the dying High Warden. They added pressure to an already complicated political landscape rather than collapsing every disputed future into one inheritance.

value.title: The Summer Without Swallows
value.summary: The event remembered as the Summer Without Swallows disrupted familiar seasonal expectations. In affected districts, growers reported altered insect activity and reduced bird arrivals. Some places experienced the absence sharply; reports from other places were incomplete or contradictory. Swallowwatch's older notebooks became valuable comparison material. Observer Enna Brin requested accounts of ordinary years as well as dramatic failures. Prophets and sellers of expensive remedies preferred simpler explanations, and several public claims travelled farther than the evidence supporting them. The loss affected work, food, and the feeling of a season arriving correctly. People who seldom agreed about politics noticed the quiet beneath familiar eaves. Returning birds in some places brought relief without proving that every disrupted pattern had recovered.

entities.name: The Porch at the Last Mile

value.title: The Porch at the Last Mile
value.summary: Near Bramblebridge's approach on the Lantern Road, host Dessa Kell added a covered porch where carriers could wait, repair straps, and compare local information before entering town. The Last Mile Porch served a practical arrival point at the road's end; it did not extend the Lantern Road beyond Bramblebridge under the same name. Visitors exchanged directions, warnings about temporary closures, and news of households farther away. A message board carried requests for deliveries and repairs. Hosts removed claims they could show were false while marking uncertain reports rather than presenting every rumour as fact. The porch grew familiar through repeated use. A traveller might remember a conversation there more clearly than the important building they had come to visit. Its household depended on paid food and lodging nearby, and keeping the waiting space available required labour.

value.title: The Open Ledger Room
value.summary: At Highmead, disputes over old obligations brought clerks, craftspeople, and household representatives together in the Open Ledger Room. Reader Samin Vell taught visitors how to compare dates, seals, units, renewals, and copies before drawing conclusions from an impressive document. Some younger officials admired the Lantern Concord's apparent administrative consistency. The room's collections showed useful shared practices alongside evidence of coercion, exclusion, and claims made stronger simply because they fitted the accepted forms. The teaching did not produce agreement about the Concord. It gave people better questions. A seven-sided seal could identify a tradition, but authority still depended on provenance, adoption, jurisdiction, and later history. The difference became increasingly important as questionable sealed instruments circulated.

value.title: Two Workshops through One Winter
value.summary: Ashglass House in Istravel and keepers of the older light panes near Seln exchanged repair notes through carriers already moving ordinary goods. A shipment of compatible backing material reached the northern workshops late, delaying work until the coldest part of the season. Glass repairer Mera Dorr and keeper Ilren Sorr agreed to complete a smaller repair that existing materials could support. The restored pane gave limited daylight at shared worktables. A donor who had expected a spectacular reopening instead attended a meal served beside ordinary lamps. Both workshops kept copies of what had actually been altered. Their correspondence also included recipes, complaints about freight charges, and news of pupils. A practical exchange became a friendship between households that had never met in full.

value.title: The Orchard that Counted Birds
value.summary: Growers in Bellafont established Swallowwatch Orchard, a working plot where gardener Tessa Brin recorded flowering, insect activity, bird arrivals, and yields. Most entries were mundane. Neighbours contributed observations because comparisons helped them understand why adjoining plots behaved differently. The records included mistakes, missed days, and disagreements over names for insects and plants. Tessa retained corrections alongside the first observations. Income came from fruit and propagation stock, with a small contribution for keeping the shared notes. The orchard became a pleasant stopping place for travellers interested in growing things. Its most useful legacy was a run of ordinary years against which later disruption could be compared. Nobody founded it knowing that the Summer Without Swallows would make such comparisons urgent.

entities.name: The Tables after the Council Meeting

value.title: The Tables after the Council Meeting
value.summary: In the Seven Lamps League, interpreters and representatives arriving from distant communities often had little time to compare what they had heard in formal sessions. Host Jori Amat rented the Long Table Rooms, offering meals, modest lodging, and a place to discuss the day's proceedings in several languages. Some delegates remembered the older compromise known as the Meal Between Minutes. Their informal meals echoed that incident without restoring the procedural protection later chairmen had removed. A conversation over supper could prepare a petition; it could not guarantee that the council would hear it. The rooms became useful to small delegations unable to hire permanent agents. They also attracted intermediaries selling introductions. Jori's household had to distinguish paid services from claims that buying a meal purchased influence.
